question: A 2720-g (6-lb) female newborn delivered at 35 weeks’ gestation starts vomiting and becomes inconsolable 48 hours after birth. The newborn has not passed her first stool yet. Examination shows abdominal distention and high-pitched bowel sounds. A water-soluble contrast enema study shows microcolon. Serum studies show increased levels of immunoreactive trypsinogen. Which of the following is the most likely additional laboratory finding?

options.opa: Decreased hydrogen ion concentration in renal collecting duct
options.opb: Increased chloride concentration in alveolar fluid
options.opd: Increased bicarbonate concentration in pancreatic secretions

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Meconium ileus" -> "obstruction of the small intestine" -> "abnormal bowel movements" -> "microcolon on imaging" -> "increased levels of immunoreactive trypsinogen" -> "possible increased chloride concentration in sweat" -> 70% CHAIN: "Meconium ileus" -> "obstruction of the small intestine" -> "abnormal bowel movements" -> "microcolon on imaging" -> "increased levels of immunoreactive trypsinogen" -> "possible increased sodium concentration in sweat" -> 70%
enhanced_information: In a newborn with meconium ileus, increased levels of immunoreactive trypsinogen suggest cystic fibrosis. This condition can lead to increased chloride concentration in sweat, making option e (Increased sodium concentration in sweat) more likely than the other options.
analysis: The core medical principle here is the association between increased levels of immunoreactive trypsinogen in a newborn with meconium ileus and cystic fibrosis. Cystic fibrosis leads to increased chloride concentration in sweat. Given this information, the most likely additional laboratory finding would be increased sodium concentration in sweat.
